\subsection{Confirmatory: the limit tracks periodicity, not length}

Figure~\ref{fig:main}(a) is the paper's sharpest test. Each control carries its
twin's carrier and word count, the $k$ copies of one word becoming non-adjacent
distinct ones. Were the failure about length, attention span, exposure bias or a
duration budget, the two curves would coincide. They do not. Below $k\!=\!6$
every model is essentially exact; above it, repeated items are rendered with a
median count error of \ErrRepCk{}\% per checkpoint against \ErrCtl{}\%
$[\ErrCtlLo{},\ErrCtlHi{}]$ for controls ($n=\ErrCtlN{}$), at every $k$ to $32$
and for every model. The contrast is sharpest in exactly-correct renderings:
\ExactCtl{}\% for controls against \ExactRep{}\% for their twins. Controls are not
perfect (\CtlMissPct{}\% carry genuine truncations) but they are exact where
their twins are not.

\emph{Our \NModels{} checkpoints are only \NFamilies{} architecture families},
so we model the clustering rather than count checkpoints. By family the gap is
\FamExact{} points $[\FamExactLo{},\FamExactHi{}]$, all three positive; by
checkpoint \CkExact{} $[\CkExactLo{},\CkExactHi{}]$, positive in all
\CkExactNPos{} --- including the checkpoint whose median-error gap is zero,
which still renders repeated items exactly \CkRevExact{} points less often than
its controls (Table~\ref{tab:models}). A mixed-effects linear probability model
with architecture as a random effect, checkpoint nested inside it, stimulus
crossed and a family-varying arm slope puts the gap at \MixArm{} points;
\MixAllClear{} six interval constructions exclude zero, the widest ---
cluster-robust at the checkpoint level --- being $[\MixLo{},\MixHi{}]$. Partial
pooling answers the question three families cannot answer directly: the
posterior predictive gap for an architecture \emph{outside} the panel is
\BayesNewFam{} points $[\BayesNewFamLo{},\BayesNewFamHi{}]$,
$P(\text{gap}>0)=\BayesNewFamP{}$ --- enough to place the effect, not enough to
exclude a fourth architecture that does not show it, and under the widest prior
on the group-level scales that interval does touch zero
($\BayesWidePriorLo{}$, $P=\BayesWidePriorP{}$). We then acquired a fourth
architecture and can report the prediction's outcome. CosyVoice~2, whose
alignment supervision makes it the design most likely to be immune, renders
repeated text exactly \CosyRep{}\% of the time against \CosyCtl{}\% for its
controls ($n=\CosyN{}$): a gap of \CosyGap{} points, inside the predicted
interval and near its \BayesNewFam{} mean, from a fit committed before the
checkpoint's first waveform existed (S16 timestamps it). That interval is wide,
and the agreement is closer than it entitles us to expect. Across \SpecN{} specifications
spanning every forking choice we made --- exclusion rules, $k$ threshold, cycled
against never-cycled controls, seed subset, aggregation level and outcome
definition --- the gap runs \SpecLo{}--\SpecHi{} points and none reverses its
sign (S11).

Above $k\!=\!8$ the control's fillers cycle a pool of eight, making the contrast
period-$1$ against period-$8$ rather than periodic against aperiodic.
Re-generating $k=12\ldots32$ from a never-cycled $146$-word pool leaves the
dissociation at \ApMidGap{} points against \ApCycGap{} for cycled controls over
the same range ($n=\ApMidN{}$): the residual is worth \ApCost{} points, not the
bulk of the gap.

\subsection{Confirmatory: not the decoding rule, the judge, or our exclusions}

The families ship repetition penalties differing by an order of magnitude, and a
penalty suppresses repeated tokens directly. Swept on \PenNArch{} architectures
the deficit stays put (XTTS-v2 \PenRepLo{}--\PenRepHi{}\% exact over a
\PenFold{}-fold range, Qwen3-TTS-0.6B \PenQRepLo{}--\PenQRepHi{}\% over
\PenQFold{}-fold, S15), and the \PenNoneN{} Llasa checkpoints pass \emph{no}
penalty and show it at full size, \PenNoneRep{}\% against \PenNoneCtl{}\%. Nor
is it sampling: greedy decoding gives \GreedyGap{} points against
\GreedySampGap{} sampled, at $0$\% cap-hit in both arms (S22). Nor our
exclusions: with every rule off the gap is \ExSensAll{} points against
\ExSensPanel{} (S18), and the budget rule --- the only one falling unevenly ---
removes \ExclCapRep{}\% of repeated generations against \ExclCapCtl{}\% of
controls, working against the contrast.

Nor is it the recogniser, the objection this design most has to answer: CTC
blank-collapse merges adjacent identical words, depressing repeated counts and
not control counts --- a judge-side artifact with the effect's own periodicity
signature. Re-scoring the \emph{same} audio with
\IndNJudges{} recognisers --- a second CTC model with different
pretraining, a robust-finetuned one, and Whisper, whose autoregressive decoder
has no blank-collapse mechanism at all --- leaves the gap at
\IndGapLo{}--\IndGapHi{} points, positive in all \IndNCkPos{} of \IndNCk{}
checkpoints and every family under every judge. Decisive is which arm moves:
across them the repeated arm's exact rate spans \IndRepSpread{} points
(\IndRepLo{}--\IndRepHi{}\%) against the control arm's \IndCtlSpread{}.
Changing the scorer moves the arm the models get \emph{right} --- word error
rate --- and leaves the arm they get wrong fixed, where a judge-side collapse
predicts the reverse. Disagreements do concentrate on repeated items, but with
the \emph{opposite} sign to the confound --- $+\IndAsym{}$ where the artifact
requires $\IndAsymThresh{}$ --- so our judge under-states the deficit rather
than manufacturing it (S14). VITS~\cite{kim2021vits}
shows \emph{no} dissociation through the same recogniser on the same strings
(\VitsRep{}\% against \VitsCtl{}\%, $n=90$, a gap of \VitsGap{} against the
panel's $+\ARPoolGap{}$), and not for want of competence: at
$k\!=\!6\text{--}8$ it renders \NonARMidRep{}\% against \NonARMidCtl{}\%, the
other way round (S13). Blank-collapse would have depressed its repeated items
too.

F5-TTS~\cite{chen2024f5tts}, flow-matching rather than recurrent, \emph{does}
show it: \FivettsRep{}\% against \FivettsCtl{}\%, $+\FivettsGap{}$, growing
with $k$ as the panel's does. Absence of an autoregressive decoder confers no
immunity, and we withdraw the architectural claim an earlier draft made. What
plausibly separates the two is where the count must live: VITS gives each input token its own duration, while F5-TTS estimates
one total duration and so must represent how much speech to make. Supplying
F5-TTS the duration a correct rendering takes splits the deficit: below
$k\!=\!\DurSplit{}$ it lifts exact renderings \DurLoFree{}\% to
\DurLoFixed{}\% ($n=\DurLoN{}$), at or above it the gain is \DurHiGain{}
($n=\DurHiN{}$). Handed the right length the model still cannot place
thirty-two repetitions inside it (S13). CosyVoice~2 says the same from the other direction: it
\emph{over}-produces (median $+\CosyMedErr{}$\% where the panel undershoots) at
a \CosyCapHit{}\% cap-hit rate, making about the right amount of speech and
still losing the count; its repetition-aware sampling rule does not prevent it.
S20 sets out three rivals we cannot exclude.

\subsection{Exploratory: past the ladder, the count levels off}

Two analyses decided on after the results above, from which we claim little;
S16 dates both. Within $k\le32$ the deficit is \emph{proportional}, not
saturating (RSS \ShapePropSSE{} against \ShapeSatSSE{}), so no counting horizon
lies inside this ladder; extending to $k\!\le\!128$ lowers the fitted saturation
scale \HzRatio{}-fold for repeated text, but form-dependently
(\HzFormLo{}--\HzFormHi{}) and not unanimously (\HzRevNames{} inverts it).
Repetition also slows state acquisition without halting it (capacity gain a
median factor \CapRatio{} of the control's). Neither result distinguishes a
counting horizon from any saturating process (Fig.~\ref{fig:main}(b,c); S8,
S10, S17).
